speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: asked the Prime Minister with the advent and drive towards the use of artificial intelligence and autonomous machines, whether new laws and regulations will be promulgated or existing ones reviewed to ensure we address the issues of ethics, morality, provision of kill switches as well as liability.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Prime Minister what policy principles and legal frameworks are being developed to update Singapore's governance and laws to address the issues arising from autonomous algorithms and devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This progressive testing allows developers to advance the technology without exposing other road users to safety risks.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Conceptually, this is similar to how a human driver has to be trained and tested before being given a driving licence.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Developers are also required to share key data with authorities to allow them to monitor the progress of the trials.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In the Government, we have developed machine learning algorithms that can detect and identify trading accounts suspected of syndicated activities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is unlike AVs, where there are issues of physical safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, we still need to rigorously test the software before use, as well as maintain and update the AI engine continuously, by performing human checks on the results from time to time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, before any account is suspended, there will still be a human process to check through and ensure that the punitive action is justified.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In other sectors, the Infocommunications Media Development Authority (IMDA) is working with sectoral regulators to discuss issues of AI governance and study the policy and legal implications.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: AI is a key enabler of Smart Nation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To exploit its use and manage its risks well, we need people with a deep understanding of the technology.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We intend to continue to raise such capabilities within the Government, industry and our research and development (R&D) institutions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is because there are growing concerns on various issues, such as liability, privacy, consent, safety, security, diversity as well as transparency.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is likely to be an ongoing discussion and attempt to look at the issues that are thrown up by new forms of technology, such as AI.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue is to make sure that we make this process fit into the existing domain's specific laws, operational issues and regulations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we have a multitude of issues going on.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Smart Nation Office will continue to study the matter and, especially as new technology and technological opportunities become available, we will continue to become engaged with the various regulations and domain-specific partners.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have three illustrations for the Senior Minister of State's consideration.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What is the impact for competition law if trading algorithms start to collude?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, would there be a role for more aspirational principles of AI, such as studying, say, Isaac Asimov's Laws of Robotics?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the first question, indeed, we are continually studying various frameworks and trying to draw up drawer plans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: AI is a big basket of different types of technologies and opportunities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is a plan or strategy for the investment around R&D.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But in terms of the regulatory and legislative space, we will have to look at the capability and its impact on the various domains.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: AI, in today's use, is what we call "weak AI" or task-specific AI.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, any criminal issue, we would have to ask the legal faculty around us, but I presume will be directed at the person who owns, operates or benefits from such a device or tool of technology.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The hon Member's third question was about the aspirational issues around AI and Asimov's Laws of Robotics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We think it has a significant possibility of enabling both the Smart Nation vision as well as significant benefits for our economy and society over the next 20 years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As for Asimov's Laws, they are a fictional device used in science fiction, but nevertheless inspiring for how we should think about these types of problems.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Neither have we the technical capability to programme in such laws today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But they are a useful thought experiment about how we should think about the regulations around this space.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Of note, the literary device of Asimov's Laws in his writing was often used as a way to describe what happens when they fail and what happens when poor regulations or poorly thought-out laws fail in terms of the opportunities around robotics and AI.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, in much of the literature, the day was rescued by Dr Susan Calvin, who was a brilliant engineer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think the salient lesson is that if we can recruit more females, more young women into engineering, it would serve our Smart Nation and AI vision far more than the use of his three laws today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Coming back to non-fictional issues, Mr Zainal Sapari.
